subModules.title: Reading Mission: The Best Places & The Most Amazing Records
subModules.grammarFocus: Superlative adjectives: the + -est (short adjectives), the most + adjective (long adjectives), irregular forms (the best, the worst)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Adjectives for describing extremes, places, food, experiences, and world records

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a fun passage about amazing world records and the best places to visit. You will learn how to understand superlative adjectives when you see them in a text. Superlatives help us talk about the number one thing in a group — the tallest, the best, the most exciting! By the end of this mission, you will feel confident reading short texts that use superlative adjectives. Let's discover the most amazing facts together!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Superlative adjective patterns: 'the + adjective-est' for short adjectives (the tallest, the biggest), 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives (the most exciting, the most beautiful), and irregular superlatives (the best, the worst, the farthest).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Adjectives describing size, height, quality, taste, cost, and excitement. Nouns related to places, food, buildings, and world records.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the passage first to understand the main topic. Then scan for superlative adjectives (look for 'the' followed by '-est' words or 'the most'). This helps you quickly find the key facts and comparisons in the text.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about world records and amazing places.
Identify superlative adjectives in a reading text and understand what is being compared.
Recognize the difference between 'the + -est' and 'the most + adjective' patterns in context.
Answer comprehension questions about specific details using information from the passage.
Build confidence reading simple English texts that describe extremes and favorites.

contextWarmup.prompt: Read this sentence: 'The Nile is the longest river in the world.' What does 'the longest' tell us about the Nile?
options: The Nile is longer than ALL other rivers — it is number one.
The Nile is longer than one other river.
The Nile is a short river.
contextWarmup.explanation: Great job! 'The longest' is a superlative adjective. It means the Nile is number one — it is longer than ALL other rivers in the world. Superlatives always compare one thing to everything else in a group.

rules: When you see 'the' + a word ending in '-est' (like 'the tallest', 'the oldest', 'the biggest'), this is a superlative for a short adjective. It means this thing is number one in its group.
When you see 'the most' + an adjective (like 'the most exciting', 'the most beautiful', 'the most expensive'), this is a superlative for a long adjective. It also means number one.
Some superlatives are irregular and do not follow the normal rules: 'good' becomes 'the best', 'bad' becomes 'the worst', and 'far' becomes 'the farthest'. You need to memorize these special forms.
Superlatives ALWAYS use 'the' before them. If you see a comparison without 'the', it is probably not a superlative. Look for 'the' as your signal word!
After a superlative, you often see 'in' (for places and groups) or 'of' (for a specific set). For example: 'the best restaurant in the city' or 'the tallest of all my friends'.

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners confuse comparative forms (bigger, more exciting) with superlative forms (the biggest, the most exciting). When reading, remember: comparatives compare TWO things and do NOT use 'the'. Superlatives compare THREE or more things and ALWAYS use 'the'. If you see 'the' + '-est' or 'the most', you know it is a superlative!
commonTrap.wrong: Reading 'She is taller than her sister' and thinking 'taller' is a superlative.
commonTrap.correct: Recognizing that 'taller' compares only two people (comparative), while 'the tallest' compares one person to everyone else (superlative).

sections.title: Reading Passage: My Amazing World Records Book

content.context: A student named Rina writes a short blog post about her favorite world records book. She shares the most interesting facts she has learned.
content.text:
Hi! My name is Rina. I love reading about world records. My dad gave me a book called 'Amazing World Records' for my birthday. It is the best gift I have ever received!

Do you know that the cheetah is the fastest animal on land? It can run very fast! And Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. I want to see it one day.

My favorite chapter is about food. The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars! Can you believe that? I think the most delicious food is my mom's fried rice. It is not the most expensive, but it is the best!

The book also says that the Amazon is the longest river in South America. And the blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean. These are the most amazing facts I have ever read. I want to learn more!

highlights.note: Irregular superlative: good → the best. This means the number one gift of all.
Short adjective superlative: fast → the fastest. One syllable + 'the -est'.
Short adjective superlative: high → the highest. Notice 'the' before the superlative.
Long adjective superlative: expensive → the most expensive. Two or more syllables use 'the most'.
Long adjective superlative: delicious → the most delicious.
Short adjective superlative: long → the longest.
Short adjective superlative: big → the biggest. Notice the double 'g' before '-est'.
Long adjective superlative: amazing → the most amazing.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Rina shares interesting superlative facts from her world records book.
Rina talks about her school and her teachers.
Rina describes her vacation to Mount Everest.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is mainly about Rina's world records book and the amazing superlative facts she learned from it, such as the fastest animal, the highest mountain, and the most expensive pizza. She does not talk about school or a vacation to Mount Everest.

detailQuestions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the fastest animal on land?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage clearly states: 'the cheetah is the fastest animal on land.' The blue whale is described as the biggest animal in the ocean, not the fastest on land.

detailQuestions.prompt: What does Rina think is the most delicious food?
detailQuestions.explanation: Rina says: 'I think the most delicious food is my mom's fried rice.' She mentions the expensive pizza as a fun fact, but she thinks her mom's cooking is the best!

detailQuestions.prompt: What is the biggest animal in the ocean, according to the passage?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'the blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean.' The cheetah is the fastest animal on land, not in the ocean. Sharks are not mentioned in the passage.

detailQuestions.prompt: Who gave Rina the world records book?
detailQuestions.explanation: Rina writes: 'My dad gave me a book called Amazing World Records for my birthday.' Her dad gave her the book as a birthday gift.

questions.question: In the passage, Rina says the book is 'the best gift.' What does 'the best' mean here?
options: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
It is a good gift, but not the number one gift.
It is a bad gift that she does not like.
questions.answer: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
questions.explanation: 'The best' is the superlative form of 'good.' It means this gift is number one — it is better than ALL other gifts Rina has ever received. Superlatives always describe the top item in a group.

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses a superlative for a LONG adjective?
options: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
The cheetah is the fastest animal on land.
The Amazon is the longest river in South America.
questions.answer: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
questions.explanation: 'Expensive' is a long adjective (three syllables), so it uses 'the most + adjective' to form the superlative: 'the most expensive.' The other two sentences use 'the -est' because 'fast' and 'long' are short adjectives.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.' What pattern does 'the highest' follow?
questions.answer: The + short adjective + -est (the highest).
questions.explanation: 'High' is a short adjective (one syllable), so its superlative form is 'the highest' — following the pattern 'the + adjective-est.' We do NOT say 'the most highest' because that is a double superlative and is incorrect.

questions.question: According to the passage, why does Rina think her mom's fried rice is special?
options: Because she thinks it is the most delicious food, even though it is not the most expensive.
Because it is the most expensive food in the world.
Because her dad made it for her birthday.
questions.answer: Because she thinks it is the most delicious food, even though it is not the most expensive.
questions.explanation: Rina says: 'I think the most delicious food is my mom's fried rice. It is not the most expensive, but it is the best!' She loves it for the taste, not the price.

questions.question: Choose the CORRECT superlative sentence based on what you learned in this reading mission.
options: The blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean.
The blue whale is most biggest animal in the ocean.
The blue whale is bigger animal in the ocean.
questions.answer: The blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean.
questions.explanation: 'Big' is a short adjective, so the superlative is 'the biggest' (the + adjective-est). 'Most biggest' is wrong because you cannot use 'most' and '-est' together. 'Bigger' is a comparative form, not a superlative — it compares only two things.

questions.question: In the passage, Rina mentions several superlative facts. How many different superlative adjectives can you find in the whole passage?
options: More than five different superlative adjectives.
questions.answer: More than five different superlative adjectives.
questions.explanation: The passage contains many superlative adjectives: the best, the fastest, the highest, the most expensive, the most delicious, the longest, the biggest, and the most amazing. That is eight superlatives — definitely more than five!

questions.question: Which word ALWAYS comes before a superlative adjective in English?
questions.answer: the
questions.explanation: Superlative adjectives ALWAYS need 'the' before them. We say 'the tallest,' 'the best,' 'the most exciting' — never 'a tallest' or 'very tallest.' The word 'the' signals that we are talking about the number one item in a group.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: The Best Places and World Records

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear two friends, Sarah and Kevin, talking about amazing places they have visited and world records they know. They use superlative adjectives to compare things in a group of three or more. Listen for words like 'the tallest', 'the longest', 'the most exciting', and 'the best'. Short adjectives add '-est' (tall becomes the tallest). Long adjectives use 'the most' before them (exciting becomes the most exciting). Some adjectives are irregular, like 'good' which becomes 'the best'. Pay close attention to the word 'the' before superlatives and the endings '-est' or the phrase 'the most'.
learningObjectives: Identify superlative adjectives when you hear them in natural spoken English.
Understand the difference between short superlatives (the tallest, the longest) and long superlatives (the most exciting, the most interesting).
Recognize irregular superlatives such as 'the best' and 'the biggest' in conversation.
Understand a conversation about places and world records using superlative forms.

keyPhrases.note: Short adjective 'tall' adds '-est' to become 'tallest'. Always use 'the' before a superlative.
Long adjective 'exciting' uses 'the most' before it. We do not add '-est' to long adjectives.
Short adjective 'long' adds '-est' to become 'longest'. Used to compare one thing with all others in a group.
Short adjective 'high' adds '-est' to become 'highest'. Describes something above all others.
Irregular superlative. 'Good' does not become 'goodest'. It changes to 'the best'.
Short adjective 'big' doubles the final consonant and adds '-est' to become 'biggest'.

connectedSpeech.slow: It was the most exciting experience.
connectedSpeech.fast: It wuz thuh most exciting experience.
connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'was' reduces to 'wuz' with a schwa sound. The word 'the' before a consonant sounds like 'thuh'. The 't' in 'exciting' can sound like a quick 'd' or tap sound.

connectedSpeech.slow: It is the tallest building in the city.
connectedSpeech.fast: It's thuh tallest building in thuh city.
connectedSpeech.slowIpa: /ɪt ɪz ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈbɪldɪŋ ɪn ðə ˈsɪti/
connectedSpeech.fastIpa: /ɪts ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈbɪldɪŋ ɪn ðə ˈsɪɾi/
connectedSpeech.note: In natural speech, 'it is' contracts to 'it's'. The word 'the' reduces to a quick 'thuh'. The 't' in 'city' often sounds like a quick tap.

connectedSpeech.slow: Do you know the longest river in the world?
connectedSpeech.fast: D'you know thuh longest river in thuh world?
connectedSpeech.slowIpa: /duː juː nəʊ ðə ˈlɒŋɡɪst ˈrɪvər ɪn ðə wɜːld/
connectedSpeech.fastIpa: /dʒə noʊ ðə ˈlɒŋɡɪst ˈrɪvər ɪn ðə wɜːld/
connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'do you' blends together and sounds like 'dju' or 'djuh'. This is very common in everyday English conversation.

connectedSpeech.slow: Mount Everest is the highest mountain.
connectedSpeech.fast: Mount Everest is thuh highest mountain.
connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, the second syllable of 'Everest' shortens. The 't' at the end of 'mountain' often becomes a glottal stop, so it sounds like 'moun-n'.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: The Best, The Biggest, The Most Amazing!

content.summary: In this writing blueprint, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs using superlative adjectives. Superlatives help you say something is number one in a group. You will use 'the + adjective-est' for short adjectives and 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives. You will also learn the irregular forms: the best, the worst, and the farthest. Let's build strong superlative sentences step by step!

blueprintItems.title: Short Adjective Superlatives (1 syllable)
blueprintItems.example: My dad is the tallest person in my family.

blueprintItems.title: Long Adjective Superlatives (2+ syllables)
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + is/are + the most + adjective + noun/place.
blueprintItems.example: This book is the most interesting book in the library.

blueprintItems.title: Irregular Superlatives
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + is/are + the best / the worst / the farthest + noun/place.
blueprintItems.example: She is the best student in our class.

blueprintItems.title: Adding a Group or Place with 'in' or 'of'
blueprintItems.formula: Superlative sentence + in the world / in my class / of all.
blueprintItems.example: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use 'the' before a superlative adjective.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She is tallest girl in the class.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She is the tallest girl in the class.
mechanicsRules.why: Superlative adjectives always need 'the' before them. Without 'the', the sentence is not correct.

mechanicsRules.rule: Double the last consonant for short adjectives ending in consonant-vowel-consonant (CVC) before adding -est.
mechanicsRules.why: For short adjectives like 'big' (consonant-vowel-consonant), you must double the last letter before adding -est: big → biggest.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'the most' for long adjectives (2 or more syllables). Do NOT add -est to long adjectives.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: This is the most beautiful park.
mechanicsRules.why: Long adjectives like 'beautiful' and 'expensive' use 'the most' before them. You never add -est to long adjectives.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first word of every sentence and end with a period.
mechanicsRules.badExample: mount everest is the highest mountain
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Mount Everest is the highest mountain.
mechanicsRules.why: Every sentence must start with a capital letter. Proper nouns like 'Mount Everest' always start with capital letters. Every sentence must end with a period.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: The Best & The Most Exciting — Superlative Talk

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise saying superlative adjectives out loud. Superlatives use 'the + adjective-est' for short words (the tallest, the biggest) and 'the most + adjective' for longer words (the most beautiful, the most exciting). When you speak, you need to stress the superlative word clearly so your listener understands which thing is number one in the group. Pay attention to the word 'the' — it is usually short and weak (/ðə/) before consonants, but slightly longer (/ðiː/) before vowels. Practise saying full sentences with confidence and clear rhythm.
content.audioGuidance: When you say superlative sentences, make the key adjective louder and slightly slower. For example, in 'the TALL-est building', stress 'TALL'. In 'the MOST ex-CI-ting sport', stress both 'MOST' and the stressed syllable of the adjective ('CI'). Use falling intonation at the end of statements: 'It is the biggest animal in the world.' ↘ Use rising intonation for yes/no questions: 'Is it the most expensive restaurant?' ↗ Keep 'the' quick and soft — do not over-pronounce it.

pillars.name: Superlative Stress Patterns
pillars.target: Correctly stress superlative adjectives in spoken sentences
pillars.explanation: Short superlatives like 'tallest', 'biggest', 'fastest' keep the stress on the first syllable: TALL-est, BIG-gest, FAST-est. For 'the most + adjective' forms, give a small stress to 'most' and then stress the main syllable of the adjective: the MOST beau-TI-ful. Practise tapping your hand on the stressed syllable.

pillars.name: Weak 'the' and Linking
pillars.explanation: In natural speech, 'the' before a consonant sound is weak: /ðə/. Before a vowel sound it becomes /ðiː/. For example: /ðə ˈbɪɡɪst/ (the biggest) vs. /ðiː ˈoʊldɪst/ (the oldest). Link 'the' smoothly to the next word without a pause.

pillars.name: Falling Intonation for Superlative Statements
pillars.target: Use natural falling intonation when stating superlative facts
pillars.explanation: When you make a statement with a superlative, your voice should go down at the end. This shows you are giving information, not asking a question. Example: 'Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.' ↘ Practise letting your pitch drop on the last word.

pillars.name: Clear Articulation of -est Ending
pillars.target: Pronounce the -est suffix clearly without dropping sounds
pillars.explanation: The ending '-est' should sound like /ɪst/ or /əst/. Do not skip the 't' at the end. Say 'fast-est' not 'faste'. Also remember spelling changes: big → biggest (double 'g'), happy → happiest (y → i). These spelling changes do not change the pronunciation rule — still stress the first syllable.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress stays on 'TALL' when we add '-est'. The word 'the' before it is weak and quick. Say: /ðə ˈtɔːlɪst/.
The stress remains on 'BIG'. Notice the double 'g' in spelling, but in speech just keep the stress on the first syllable: /ðə ˈbɪɡɪst/.
With long adjectives we add 'the most' before the adjective. Stress both 'MOST' and the main syllable of the adjective 'CI'. Say: /ðə ˈmoʊst ɪkˈsaɪtɪŋ/.
'Beautiful' has three syllables with stress on 'BEAU'. When we add 'the most', give a secondary stress to 'MOST' and keep the primary stress on 'BEAU': /ðə ˈmoʊst ˈbjuːtɪfəl/.
Stress stays on 'FAST'. The '-est' ending is unstressed. Be sure to pronounce the final /t/ in 'fastest': /ðə ˈfæstɪst/.

drills.targetText: The tallest building in the city is near the park.
drills.phonetic: /ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈbɪldɪŋ ɪn ðə ˈsɪti ɪz nɪr ðə pɑːrk/
drills.focus: Stress on 'tallest' and falling intonation at end
drills.hint: Make 'TALL' louder than '-est'. Let your voice go down on 'park'.

drills.targetText: The biggest animal in the world is the blue whale.
drills.phonetic: /ðə ˈbɪɡɪst ˈænɪməl ɪn ðə wɜːrld ɪz ðə bluː weɪl/
drills.hint: Say 'BIG-gest' with a strong 'BIG'. Link 'in the' smoothly as /ɪnðə/.

drills.targetText: She is the most beautiful singer I know.
drills.phonetic: /ʃiː ɪz ðə ˈmoʊst ˈbjuːtɪfəl ˈsɪŋər aɪ noʊ/
drills.hint: Give a small pause after 'most' then stress 'BEAU-ti-ful'. Drop your pitch on 'know'.

drills.targetText: What is the most exciting sport to watch?
drills.phonetic: /wɒt ɪz ðə ˈmoʊst ɪkˈsaɪtɪŋ spɔːrt tə wɒtʃ/
drills.hint: This is a question, so let your voice rise slightly on 'watch?' ↗

drills.targetText: My father is the tallest person in my family.
drills.phonetic: /maɪ ˈfɑːðər ɪz ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈpɜːrsən ɪn maɪ ˈfæməli/
drills.focus: Natural rhythm with superlative in mid-sentence
drills.hint: Stress 'TALL-est' and 'family'. Keep 'in my' quick and connected.

drills.targetText: This is the cheapest restaurant in town.
drills.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz ðə ˈtʃiːpɪst ˈrɛstərɒnt ɪn taʊn/
drills.hint: Start 'cheapest' with a clear /tʃ/ sound, like 'ch' in 'cheese'. Stress 'CHEAP'.

roleplay.context: You are chatting with Mr. Khoirul about your favourite things and world records. He will ask you superlative questions and you should answer using 'the + adjective-est' or 'the most + adjective' forms. Speak clearly and use falling intonation for your answers.

turns.translation: Halo! Hari ini kita akan berbicara tentang hal-hal terbaik dan paling menarik. Apa tempat terindah yang pernah kamu kunjungi?

turns.text: The most beautiful place I've visited is Bali. The beaches are amazing.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about the best holiday you have ever had. Use superlative adjectives to describe your experience. Follow the three story points below and speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell a story! Think about the best holiday you have ever had. Where did you go? What was the best thing about it? Tell me your story using superlative adjectives like 'the best', 'the most beautiful', or 'the happiest'.
storyPoints: Say where you went and why it was the best holiday.
Describe the most beautiful or the most interesting thing you saw there.
Explain how you felt — for example, it was the happiest day of your life.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The best holiday I have ever had was in Bali. I saw the most beautiful sunset on the beach. It was the happiest day of my life.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə bɛst ˈhɒlɪdeɪ aɪ hæv ˈɛvər hæd wɒz ɪn ˈbɑːli. aɪ sɔː ðə moʊst ˈbjuːtɪfəl ˈsʌnsɛt ɒn ðə biːtʃ. ɪt wɒz ðə ˈhæpiɪst deɪ ɒv maɪ laɪf/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use 'the' before every superlative. Stress the adjective: 'the BEST', 'the MOST BEAU-ti-ful', 'the HAP-pi-est'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using superlative adjectives in connected speech. You need to combine 'the + -est' for short adjectives and 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives while maintaining natural rhythm and falling intonation at the end of each sentence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your school or workplace. Use superlative adjectives to compare people and things. Follow the three story points below.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now tell me about your school or your workplace. Who is the smartest person? What is the most difficult subject or task? Use superlative adjectives and speak clearly.
storyPoints: Describe who is the smartest or the funniest person at your school or workplace.
Talk about the most difficult subject or the hardest task you do.
Say what is the best thing about your school or workplace.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The smartest person in my class is my friend Rina. The most difficult subject is mathematics. The best thing about my school is the friendly teachers.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈsmɑːrtɪst ˈpɜːrsən ɪn maɪ klæs ɪz maɪ frɛnd ˈriːnə. ðə moʊst ˈdɪfɪkəlt ˈsʌbdʒɪkt ɪz ˌmæθəˈmætɪks. ðə bɛst θɪŋ əˈbaʊt maɪ skuːl ɪz ðə ˈfrɛndli ˈtiːtʃərz/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'the + -est' for short adjectives (smartest, best) and 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives (most difficult). Let your voice fall at the end of each sentence.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task helps you practise superlatives in a real-life context. Describing people and things at school or work is a common A1 speaking topic. Focus on choosing the correct superlative form and stressing the key adjective.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a travel agency. The travel agent (Mr. Khoirul) is helping you choose a holiday destination. Answer his questions using superlative adjectives. Talk about the cheapest, the most popular, or the best destination.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to Happy Travel Agency! I'm here to help you find the perfect holiday. Let's talk about what kind of place you want to visit. Are you ready?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a customer at a travel agency. The travel agent will ask you about your preferences for a holiday. You need to use superlative adjectives to explain what you want — for example, the cheapest option, the most beautiful beach, or the best hotel.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the customer. Mr. Khoirul is the travel agent. He will ask you questions about your ideal holiday and you should respond using superlative forms.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I want to go to the cheapest destination. I want the most beautiful beach and the best hotel.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wɒnt tə ɡoʊ tə ðə ˈtʃiːpɪst ˌdɛstɪˈneɪʃən. aɪ wɒnt ðə moʊst ˈbjuːtɪfəl biːtʃ ænd ðə bɛst hoʊˈtɛl/
practicumQuestions.hint: When the agent asks about price, use 'the cheapest'. When he asks about scenery, use 'the most beautiful'. Stress the superlative word clearly.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises using superlatives in a practical travel conversation. At A1 level, learners should be able to express simple preferences using superlative adjectives in a service encounter.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to your friend (Mr. Khoirul) about a quiz show on TV. Discuss who was the fastest, the smartest, and who gave the most interesting answers. Use superlative adjectives in your responses.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hey! Did you watch the quiz show last night? It was so fun! Let's talk about the contestants. Who do you think was the best?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your friend are discussing a TV quiz show you both watched. You need to compare the contestants using superlative adjectives — who was the fastest, the smartest, the funniest, or who gave the most interesting answers.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a friend chatting casually. Mr. Khoirul is your friend who also watched the quiz show. Share your opinions about the contestants using superlatives.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I think the woman in the red shirt was the smartest. She gave the most interesting answers and she was the fastest.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ θɪŋk ðə ˈwʊmən ɪn ðə rɛd ʃɜːrt wɒz ðə ˈsmɑːrtɪst. ʃiː ɡeɪv ðə moʊst ˈɪntrəstɪŋ ˈænsərz ænd ʃiː wɒz ðə ˈfæstɪst/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'I think...' to give your opinion. Then add a superlative: 'the smartest', 'the fastest', 'the most interesting'. Stress the adjective clearly.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises giving opinions with superlatives in a casual conversation. Comparing people is a natural way to use superlative adjectives, and expressing opinions with 'I think' is an important A1 skill.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a restaurant with Mr. Khoirul. He is the waiter. Ask him about the menu using superlative adjectives — for example, the most popular dish, the cheapest meal, or the best dessert.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good evening! Welcome to our restaurant. Here is the menu. Do you have any questions? I can help you choose the best dish for you!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are a customer at a restaurant. The waiter will help you choose food from the menu. You should ask questions and make requests using superlative adjectives, such as 'the most popular', 'the cheapest', or 'the best'.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the restaurant customer. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. Ask him about the food using superlatives and then order something.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: What is the most popular dish? I want the cheapest meal, please. What is the best dessert you have?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wɒt ɪz ðə moʊst ˈpɒpjʊlər dɪʃ? aɪ wɒnt ðə ˈtʃiːpɪst miːl pliːz. wɒt ɪz ðə bɛst dɪˈzɜːrt juː hæv/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use rising intonation when asking questions: 'What is the most popular dish?' ↗ Use falling intonation when ordering: 'I want the cheapest meal, please.' ↘
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ordering food is a key A1 real-life scenario. This roleplay combines superlative adjectives with question forms and polite requests, helping you practise both grammar and natural intonation patterns.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul about world records. He will ask you questions about the tallest, the longest, and the most dangerous things in the world. Answer using superlative adjectives and full sentences.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's play a world records game! I will ask you questions about amazing things in the world. Try to answer using superlative adjectives. Ready? Here we go!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are playing a world records quiz game with your teacher. He asks you about the tallest mountain, the longest river, the most dangerous animal, and other world records. You answer using superlative adjectives in complete sentences.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the student answering world record questions. Mr. Khoirul is the quiz master asking about the tallest, longest, biggest, and most dangerous things in the world.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The tallest mountain in the world is Mount Everest. The longest river is the Nile. The most dangerous animal is the mosquito.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ɪz maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst. ðə ˈlɒŋɡɪst ˈrɪvər ɪz ðə naɪl. ðə moʊst ˈdeɪndʒərəs ˈænɪməl ɪz ðə məˈskiːtoʊ/
practicumQuestions.hint: For short adjectives: 'the tallest', 'the longest'. For long adjectives: 'the most dangerous'. Always start with 'The' and use a full sentence with 'is'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: World records are a fun and natural context for practising superlatives. This roleplay helps you produce complete superlative sentences with correct structure: 'The + superlative + noun + is + answer'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following superlative adjective and its meaning in a full sentence. Focus on using the correct superlative form.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's practise superlative vocabulary. Please say this word in a full sentence. The word is 'the most expensive'. Use it to describe something you know.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The most expensive phone in the shop is the newest iPhone.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə moʊst ɪkˈspɛnsɪv foʊn ɪn ðə ʃɒp ɪz ðə ˈnjuːɪst ˈaɪfoʊn/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember: 'expensive' is a long adjective, so we say 'the most expensive', not 'the expensivest'. Stress 'MOST' and 'PEN' in 'ex-PEN-sive'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill checks that you know when to use 'the most + adjective' versus 'the + adjective-est'. Long adjectives (three or more syllables, and most two-syllable adjectives) use 'the most'. Short adjectives (one syllable, some two-syllable) use '-est'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the sentence with the correct superlative grammar. Change the adjective in brackets to the correct superlative form. The sentence is: 'This is (interesting) book I have ever read.'
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's check your grammar. I will give you a sentence with an adjective. You need to change it to the superlative form and say the complete sentence. Ready? 'This is [interesting] book I have ever read.' Say the full correct sentence now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This is the most interesting book I have ever read.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz ðə moʊst ˈɪntrəstɪŋ bʊk aɪ hæv ˈɛvər rɛd/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Interesting' has four syllables, so you must use 'the most interesting', not 'the interestingest'. Don't forget 'the' before 'most'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This grammar drill tests the rule: adjectives with three or more syllables always form the superlative with 'the most + adjective'. Common errors include forgetting 'the' or trying to add '-est' to long adjectives. The structure is: subject + is/are + the most + adjective + noun.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise the syllable stress shift between the base adjective and its superlative form. Say both words clearly, stressing the correct syllable. First say 'exciting', then say 'the most exciting'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's practise syllable stress. First, say the adjective 'exciting' — the stress is on the second syllable: ex-CI-ting. Now say the superlative form: 'the most exciting' — stress both 'MOST' and 'CI'. Say both forms now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Exciting. The most exciting.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪkˈsaɪtɪŋ/ — /ðə ˈmoʊst ɪkˈsaɪtɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: In 'exciting', stress the middle syllable: ex-CI-ting. When you add 'the most', give a strong stress to 'MOST' as well. Do NOT stress 'the' — keep it weak: /ðə/.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When forming superlatives with 'the most', the stress pattern shifts because you add a new stressed word ('most') before the adjective. The adjective keeps its original stress (ex-CI-ting), but now 'MOST' also receives stress. This creates a two-stress rhythm: 'the MOST ex-CI-ting'. Practise this rhythm to sound natural.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise the difference between falling intonation (for statements) and rising intonation (for yes/no questions) when using superlative adjectives. Say both sentences clearly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise intonation. First, say this statement with falling intonation: 'Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world.' ↘ Your voice should go DOWN at the end. Now say this question with rising intonation: 'Is Mount Everest the tallest mountain in the world?' ↗ Your voice should go UP at the end. Say both sentences now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. Is Mount Everest the tallest mountain in the world?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst ɪz ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ↘/ — /ɪz maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: For the statement, let your pitch fall on 'world' ↘. For the yes/no question, let your pitch rise on 'world?' ↗. The words are almost the same, but the intonation changes the meaning completely.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation is crucial for meaning in English. Statements use falling intonation (↘) to show you are giving information. Yes/no questions use rising intonation (↗) to show you are asking for confirmation. With superlative sentences, this distinction is especially important because the same words can be a fact or a question depending on your intonation.

reading.question: In the passage, Rina says the book is 'the best gift.' What does 'the best' mean here?
options: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
It is a good gift, but not the number one gift.
It is a bad gift that she does not like.
reading.answer: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
reading.explanation: 'The best' is the superlative form of 'good.' It means this gift is number one — it is better than ALL other gifts Rina has ever received. Superlatives always describe the top item in a group.

reading.question: Which sentence from the passage uses a superlative for a LONG adjective?
options: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
The cheetah is the fastest animal on land.
The Amazon is the longest river in South America.
reading.answer: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
reading.explanation: 'Expensive' is a long adjective (three syllables), so it uses 'the most + adjective' to form the superlative: 'the most expensive.' The other two sentences use 'the -est' because 'fast' and 'long' are short adjectives.

reading.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.' What pattern does 'the highest' follow?
reading.explanation: 'High' is a short adjective (one syllable), so its superlative form is 'the highest' — following the pattern 'the + adjective-est.' We do NOT say 'the most highest' because that is a double superlative and is incorrect.

reading.question: According to the passage, why does Rina think her mom's fried rice is special?
options: Because she thinks it is the most delicious food, even though it is not the most expensive.
Because it is the most expensive food in the world.
Because her dad made it for her birthday.
reading.answer: Because she thinks it is the most delicious food, even though it is not the most expensive.
reading.explanation: Rina says: 'I think the most delicious food is my mom's fried rice. It is not the most expensive, but it is the best!' She loves it for the taste, not the price.

reading.question: Choose the CORRECT superlative sentence based on what you learned in this reading mission.

reading.answer: The blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean.
reading.explanation: 'Big' is a short adjective, so the superlative is 'the biggest' (the + adjective-est). 'Most biggest' is wrong because you cannot use 'most' and '-est' together. 'Bigger' is a comparative form, not a superlative — it compares only two things.

reading.question: In the passage, Rina mentions several superlative facts. How many different superlative adjectives can you find in the whole passage?

reading.question: Which word ALWAYS comes before a superlative adjective in English?
reading.explanation: Superlative adjectives ALWAYS need 'the' before them. We say 'the tallest,' 'the best,' 'the most exciting' — never 'a tallest' or 'very tallest.' The word 'the' signals that we are talking about the number one item in a group.

writing.prompt: Write 3 sentences about your school. Use a different superlative adjective in each sentence. Use one short adjective superlative, one long adjective superlative, and one irregular superlative.
writing.criteria: The answer must have 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must use a superlative adjective correctly. writing.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 4 sentences) about your family. Describe who is the tallest, the youngest, the best at cooking, or the most funny person. Use at least 3 superlative adjectives.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about the best holiday you have ever had. Use superlative adjectives to describe your experience. Follow the three story points below and speak for about 30 seconds.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell a story! Think about the best holiday you have ever had. Where did you go? What was the best thing about it? Tell me your story using superlative adjectives like 'the best', 'the most beautiful', or 'the happiest'.
storyPoints: Say where you went and why it was the best holiday.
Describe the most beautiful or the most interesting thing you saw there.
Explain how you felt — for example, it was the happiest day of your life.
speaking.targetSentence: The best holiday I have ever had was in Bali. I saw the most beautiful sunset on the beach. It was the happiest day of my life.
speaking.phonetic: /ðə bɛst ˈhɒlɪdeɪ aɪ hæv ˈɛvər hæd wɒz ɪn ˈbɑːli. aɪ sɔː ðə moʊst ˈbjuːtɪfəl ˈsʌnsɛt ɒn ðə biːtʃ. ɪt wɒz ðə ˈhæpiɪst deɪ ɒv maɪ laɪf/
speaking.hint: Remember to use 'the' before every superlative. Stress the adjective: 'the BEST', 'the MOST BEAU-ti-ful', 'the HAP-pi-est'.
speaking.explanation: This storytelling task practises using superlative adjectives in connected speech. You need to combine 'the + -est' for short adjectives and 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives while maintaining natural rhythm and falling intonation at the end of each sentence.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about your school or workplace. Use superlative adjectives to compare people and things. Follow the three story points below.

storyPoints: Describe who is the smartest or the funniest person at your school or workplace.
Talk about the most difficult subject or the hardest task you do.
Say what is the best thing about your school or workplace.
speaking.targetSentence: The smartest person in my class is my friend Rina. The most difficult subject is mathematics. The best thing about my school is the friendly teachers.
speaking.phonetic: /ðə ˈsmɑːrtɪst ˈpɜːrsən ɪn maɪ klæs ɪz maɪ frɛnd ˈriːnə. ðə moʊst ˈdɪfɪkəlt ˈsʌbdʒɪkt ɪz ˌmæθəˈmætɪks. ðə bɛst θɪŋ əˈbaʊt maɪ skuːl ɪz ðə ˈfrɛndli ˈtiːtʃərz/
speaking.hint: Use 'the + -est' for short adjectives (smartest, best) and 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives (most difficult). Let your voice fall at the end of each sentence.
speaking.explanation: This task helps you practise superlatives in a real-life context. Describing people and things at school or work is a common A1 speaking topic. Focus on choosing the correct superlative form and stressing the key adjective.

speaking.instruction: You are at a travel agency. The travel agent (Mr. Khoirul) is helping you choose a holiday destination. Answer his questions using superlative adjectives. Talk about the cheapest, the most popular, or the best destination.

speaking.scenarioContext: You are a customer at a travel agency. The travel agent will ask you about your preferences for a holiday. You need to use superlative adjectives to explain what you want — for example, the cheapest option, the most beautiful beach, or the best hotel.
speaking.characterRole: You are the customer. Mr. Khoirul is the travel agent. He will ask you questions about your ideal holiday and you should respond using superlative forms.

speaking.characterRole: You are a friend chatting casually. Mr. Khoirul is your friend who also watched the quiz show. Share your opinions about the contestants using superlatives.
speaking.targetSentence: I think the woman in the red shirt was the smartest. She gave the most interesting answers and she was the fastest.
speaking.phonetic: /aɪ θɪŋk ðə ˈwʊmən ɪn ðə rɛd ʃɜːrt wɒz ðə ˈsmɑːrtɪst. ʃiː ɡeɪv ðə moʊst ˈɪntrəstɪŋ ˈænsərz ænd ʃiː wɒz ðə ˈfæstɪst/
speaking.hint: Use 'I think...' to give your opinion. Then add a superlative: 'the smartest', 'the fastest', 'the most interesting'. Stress the adjective clearly.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises giving opinions with superlatives in a casual conversation. Comparing people is a natural way to use superlative adjectives, and expressing opinions with 'I think' is an important A1 skill.

speaking.instruction: You are at a restaurant with Mr. Khoirul. He is the waiter. Ask him about the menu using superlative adjectives — for example, the most popular dish, the cheapest meal, or the best dessert.
speaking.audioPrompt: Good evening! Welcome to our restaurant. Here is the menu. Do you have any questions? I can help you choose the best dish for you!
speaking.scenarioContext: You are a customer at a restaurant. The waiter will help you choose food from the menu. You should ask questions and make requests using superlative adjectives, such as 'the most popular', 'the cheapest', or 'the best'.
speaking.characterRole: You are the restaurant customer. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. Ask him about the food using superlatives and then order something.
speaking.targetSentence: What is the most popular dish? I want the cheapest meal, please. What is the best dessert you have?

speaking.hint: Use rising intonation when asking questions: 'What is the most popular dish?' ↗ Use falling intonation when ordering: 'I want the cheapest meal, please.' ↘
speaking.explanation: Ordering food is a key A1 real-life scenario. This roleplay combines superlative adjectives with question forms and polite requests, helping you practise both grammar and natural intonation patterns.

speaking.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul about world records. He will ask you questions about the tallest, the longest, and the most dangerous things in the world. Answer using superlative adjectives and full sentences.

speaking.targetSentence: The tallest mountain in the world is Mount Everest. The longest river is the Nile. The most dangerous animal is the mosquito.
speaking.phonetic: /ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ɪz maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst. ðə ˈlɒŋɡɪst ˈrɪvər ɪz ðə naɪl. ðə moʊst ˈdeɪndʒərəs ˈænɪməl ɪz ðə məˈskiːtoʊ/
speaking.hint: For short adjectives: 'the tallest', 'the longest'. For long adjectives: 'the most dangerous'. Always start with 'The' and use a full sentence with 'is'.
speaking.explanation: World records are a fun and natural context for practising superlatives. This roleplay helps you produce complete superlative sentences with correct structure: 'The + superlative + noun + is + answer'.

speaking.instruction: Say the following superlative adjective and its meaning in a full sentence. Focus on using the correct superlative form.
speaking.audioPrompt: Let's practise superlative vocabulary. Please say this word in a full sentence. The word is 'the most expensive'. Use it to describe something you know.
speaking.targetSentence: The most expensive phone in the shop is the newest iPhone.
speaking.phonetic: /ðə moʊst ɪkˈspɛnsɪv foʊn ɪn ðə ʃɒp ɪz ðə ˈnjuːɪst ˈaɪfoʊn/
speaking.hint: Remember: 'expensive' is a long adjective, so we say 'the most expensive', not 'the expensivest'. Stress 'MOST' and 'PEN' in 'ex-PEN-sive'.
speaking.explanation: This drill checks that you know when to use 'the most + adjective' versus 'the + adjective-est'. Long adjectives (three or more syllables, and most two-syllable adjectives) use 'the most'. Short adjectives (one syllable, some two-syllable) use '-est'.

speaking.instruction: Say the sentence with the correct superlative grammar. Change the adjective in brackets to the correct superlative form. The sentence is: 'This is (interesting) book I have ever read.'
speaking.audioPrompt: Now let's check your grammar. I will give you a sentence with an adjective. You need to change it to the superlative form and say the complete sentence. Ready? 'This is [interesting] book I have ever read.' Say the full correct sentence now.
speaking.targetSentence: This is the most interesting book I have ever read.
speaking.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz ðə moʊst ˈɪntrəstɪŋ bʊk aɪ hæv ˈɛvər rɛd/
speaking.hint: 'Interesting' has four syllables, so you must use 'the most interesting', not 'the interestingest'. Don't forget 'the' before 'most'.
speaking.explanation: This grammar drill tests the rule: adjectives with three or more syllables always form the superlative with 'the most + adjective'. Common errors include forgetting 'the' or trying to add '-est' to long adjectives. The structure is: subject + is/are + the most + adjective + noun.

speaking.instruction: Practise the syllable stress shift between the base adjective and its superlative form. Say both words clearly, stressing the correct syllable. First say 'exciting', then say 'the most exciting'.
speaking.audioPrompt: Let's practise syllable stress. First, say the adjective 'exciting' — the stress is on the second syllable: ex-CI-ting. Now say the superlative form: 'the most exciting' — stress both 'MOST' and 'CI'. Say both forms now.
speaking.hint: In 'exciting', stress the middle syllable: ex-CI-ting. When you add 'the most', give a strong stress to 'MOST' as well. Do NOT stress 'the' — keep it weak: /ðə/.
speaking.explanation: When forming superlatives with 'the most', the stress pattern shifts because you add a new stressed word ('most') before the adjective. The adjective keeps its original stress (ex-CI-ting), but now 'MOST' also receives stress. This creates a two-stress rhythm: 'the MOST ex-CI-ting'. Practise this rhythm to sound natural.

speaking.instruction: Practise the difference between falling intonation (for statements) and rising intonation (for yes/no questions) when using superlative adjectives. Say both sentences clearly.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now let's practise intonation. First, say this statement with falling intonation: 'Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world.' ↘ Your voice should go DOWN at the end. Now say this question with rising intonation: 'Is Mount Everest the tallest mountain in the world?' ↗ Your voice should go UP at the end. Say both sentences now.
speaking.targetSentence: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. Is Mount Everest the tallest mountain in the world?
speaking.phonetic: /maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst ɪz ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ↘/ — /ɪz maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ↗/
speaking.hint: For the statement, let your pitch fall on 'world' ↘. For the yes/no question, let your pitch rise on 'world?' ↗. The words are almost the same, but the intonation changes the meaning completely.
speaking.explanation: Intonation is crucial for meaning in English. Statements use falling intonation (↘) to show you are giving information. Yes/no questions use rising intonation (↗) to show you are asking for confirmation. With superlative sentences, this distinction is especially important because the same words can be a fact or a question depending on your intonation.

questions.question: In the passage, Rina says the book is 'the best gift.' What does 'the best' mean here?
options: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
It is a good gift, but not the number one gift.
It is a bad gift that she does not like.
questions.answer: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
questions.explanation: 'The best' is the superlative form of 'good.' It means this gift is number one — it is better than ALL other gifts Rina has ever received. Superlatives always describe the top item in a group.

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses a superlative for a LONG adjective?
options: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
The cheetah is the fastest animal on land.
The Amazon is the longest river in South America.
questions.answer: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
questions.explanation: 'Expensive' is a long adjective (three syllables), so it uses 'the most + adjective' to form the superlative: 'the most expensive.' The other two sentences use 'the -est' because 'fast' and 'long' are short adjectives.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.' What pattern does 'the highest' follow?
questions.answer: The + short adjective + -est (the highest).
questions.explanation: 'High' is a short adjective (one syllable), so its superlative form is 'the highest' — following the pattern 'the + adjective-est.' We do NOT say 'the most highest' because that is a double superlative and is incorrect.

questions.question: According to the passage, why does Rina think her mom's fried rice is special?

questions.answer: Because she thinks it is the most delicious food, even though it is not the most expensive.
questions.explanation: Rina says: 'I think the most delicious food is my mom's fried rice. It is not the most expensive, but it is the best!' She loves it for the taste, not the price.

questions.question: Choose the CORRECT superlative sentence based on what you learned in this reading mission.

The blue whale is most biggest animal in the ocean.
The blue whale is bigger animal in the ocean.
questions.answer: The blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean.
questions.explanation: 'Big' is a short adjective, so the superlative is 'the biggest' (the + adjective-est). 'Most biggest' is wrong because you cannot use 'most' and '-est' together. 'Bigger' is a comparative form, not a superlative — it compares only two things.

questions.question: In the passage, Rina mentions several superlative facts. How many different superlative adjectives can you find in the whole passage?
options: More than five different superlative adjectives.
questions.answer: More than five different superlative adjectives.
questions.explanation: The passage contains many superlative adjectives: the best, the fastest, the highest, the most expensive, the most delicious, the longest, the biggest, and the most amazing. That is eight superlatives — definitely more than five!

questions.question: Which word ALWAYS comes before a superlative adjective in English?
questions.answer: the
questions.explanation: Superlative adjectives ALWAYS need 'the' before them. We say 'the tallest,' 'the best,' 'the most exciting' — never 'a tallest' or 'very tallest.' The word 'the' signals that we are talking about the number one item in a group.

questions.prompt: Write 3 sentences about your school. Use a different superlative adjective in each sentence. Use one short adjective superlative, one long adjective superlative, and one irregular superlative.
questions.criteria: The answer must have 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must use a superlative adjective correctly. One sentence uses 'the + adjective-est', one uses 'the most + adjective', and one uses an irregular superlative (the best, the worst, or the farthest). All sentences must start with a capital letter and end with a period.
questions.sampleGoodAnswer: Mr. Andi is the tallest teacher in my school. The library is the most comfortable room in the building. My best friend is the best student in our class.

questions.instruction: Tell a short story about the best holiday you have ever had. Use superlative adjectives to describe your experience. Follow the three story points below and speak for about 30 seconds.
questions.audioPrompt: Now it's your turn to tell a story! Think about the best holiday you have ever had. Where did you go? What was the best thing about it? Tell me your story using superlative adjectives like 'the best', 'the most beautiful', or 'the happiest'.
storyPoints: Say where you went and why it was the best holiday.
Describe the most beautiful or the most interesting thing you saw there.
Explain how you felt — for example, it was the happiest day of your life.
questions.targetSentence: The best holiday I have ever had was in Bali. I saw the most beautiful sunset on the beach. It was the happiest day of my life.
questions.phonetic: /ðə bɛst ˈhɒlɪdeɪ aɪ hæv ˈɛvər hæd wɒz ɪn ˈbɑːli. aɪ sɔː ðə moʊst ˈbjuːtɪfəl ˈsʌnsɛt ɒn ðə biːtʃ. ɪt wɒz ðə ˈhæpiɪst deɪ ɒv maɪ laɪf/
questions.hint: Remember to use 'the' before every superlative. Stress the adjective: 'the BEST', 'the MOST BEAU-ti-ful', 'the HAP-pi-est'.
questions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using superlative adjectives in connected speech. You need to combine 'the + -est' for short adjectives and 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives while maintaining natural rhythm and falling intonation at the end of each sentence.

questions.instruction: Tell a short story about your school or workplace. Use superlative adjectives to compare people and things. Follow the three story points below.

Talk about the most difficult subject or the hardest task you do.
Say what is the best thing about your school or workplace.
questions.targetSentence: The smartest person in my class is my friend Rina. The most difficult subject is mathematics. The best thing about my school is the friendly teachers.
questions.phonetic: /ðə ˈsmɑːrtɪst ˈpɜːrsən ɪn maɪ klæs ɪz maɪ frɛnd ˈriːnə. ðə moʊst ˈdɪfɪkəlt ˈsʌbdʒɪkt ɪz ˌmæθəˈmætɪks. ðə bɛst θɪŋ əˈbaʊt maɪ skuːl ɪz ðə ˈfrɛndli ˈtiːtʃərz/
questions.hint: Use 'the + -est' for short adjectives (smartest, best) and 'the most + adjective' for long adjectives (most difficult). Let your voice fall at the end of each sentence.
questions.explanation: This task helps you practise superlatives in a real-life context. Describing people and things at school or work is a common A1 speaking topic. Focus on choosing the correct superlative form and stressing the key adjective.

questions.instruction: You are at a travel agency. The travel agent (Mr. Khoirul) is helping you choose a holiday destination. Answer his questions using superlative adjectives. Talk about the cheapest, the most popular, or the best destination.
questions.audioPrompt: Welcome to Happy Travel Agency! I'm here to help you find the perfect holiday. Let's talk about what kind of place you want to visit. Are you ready?
questions.scenarioContext: You are a customer at a travel agency. The travel agent will ask you about your preferences for a holiday. You need to use superlative adjectives to explain what you want — for example, the cheapest option, the most beautiful beach, or the best hotel.
questions.characterRole: You are the customer. Mr. Khoirul is the travel agent. He will ask you questions about your ideal holiday and you should respond using superlative forms.
questions.targetSentence: I want to go to the cheapest destination. I want the most beautiful beach and the best hotel.
questions.phonetic: /aɪ wɒnt tə ɡoʊ tə ðə ˈtʃiːpɪst ˌdɛstɪˈneɪʃən. aɪ wɒnt ðə moʊst ˈbjuːtɪfəl biːtʃ ænd ðə bɛst hoʊˈtɛl/
questions.hint: When the agent asks about price, use 'the cheapest'. When he asks about scenery, use 'the most beautiful'. Stress the superlative word clearly.
questions.explanation: This roleplay practises using superlatives in a practical travel conversation. At A1 level, learners should be able to express simple preferences using superlative adjectives in a service encounter.

questions.instruction: You are talking to your friend (Mr. Khoirul) about a quiz show on TV. Discuss who was the fastest, the smartest, and who gave the most interesting answers. Use superlative adjectives in your responses.
questions.audioPrompt: Hey! Did you watch the quiz show last night? It was so fun! Let's talk about the contestants. Who do you think was the best?
questions.scenarioContext: You and your friend are discussing a TV quiz show you both watched. You need to compare the contestants using superlative adjectives — who was the fastest, the smartest, the funniest, or who gave the most interesting answers.
questions.characterRole: You are a friend chatting casually. Mr. Khoirul is your friend who also watched the quiz show. Share your opinions about the contestants using superlatives.
questions.targetSentence: I think the woman in the red shirt was the smartest. She gave the most interesting answers and she was the fastest.
questions.phonetic: /aɪ θɪŋk ðə ˈwʊmən ɪn ðə rɛd ʃɜːrt wɒz ðə ˈsmɑːrtɪst. ʃiː ɡeɪv ðə moʊst ˈɪntrəstɪŋ ˈænsərz ænd ʃiː wɒz ðə ˈfæstɪst/
questions.hint: Use 'I think...' to give your opinion. Then add a superlative: 'the smartest', 'the fastest', 'the most interesting'. Stress the adjective clearly.
questions.explanation: This roleplay practises giving opinions with superlatives in a casual conversation. Comparing people is a natural way to use superlative adjectives, and expressing opinions with 'I think' is an important A1 skill.

questions.instruction: You are at a restaurant with Mr. Khoirul. He is the waiter. Ask him about the menu using superlative adjectives — for example, the most popular dish, the cheapest meal, or the best dessert.
questions.audioPrompt: Good evening! Welcome to our restaurant. Here is the menu. Do you have any questions? I can help you choose the best dish for you!
questions.scenarioContext: You are a customer at a restaurant. The waiter will help you choose food from the menu. You should ask questions and make requests using superlative adjectives, such as 'the most popular', 'the cheapest', or 'the best'.
questions.characterRole: You are the restaurant customer. Mr. Khoirul is the waiter. Ask him about the food using superlatives and then order something.
questions.targetSentence: What is the most popular dish? I want the cheapest meal, please. What is the best dessert you have?

questions.hint: Use rising intonation when asking questions: 'What is the most popular dish?' ↗ Use falling intonation when ordering: 'I want the cheapest meal, please.' ↘
questions.explanation: Ordering food is a key A1 real-life scenario. This roleplay combines superlative adjectives with question forms and polite requests, helping you practise both grammar and natural intonation patterns.

questions.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul about world records. He will ask you questions about the tallest, the longest, and the most dangerous things in the world. Answer using superlative adjectives and full sentences.
questions.audioPrompt: Let's play a world records game! I will ask you questions about amazing things in the world. Try to answer using superlative adjectives. Ready? Here we go!
questions.scenarioContext: You are playing a world records quiz game with your teacher. He asks you about the tallest mountain, the longest river, the most dangerous animal, and other world records. You answer using superlative adjectives in complete sentences.
questions.characterRole: You are the student answering world record questions. Mr. Khoirul is the quiz master asking about the tallest, longest, biggest, and most dangerous things in the world.
questions.targetSentence: The tallest mountain in the world is Mount Everest. The longest river is the Nile. The most dangerous animal is the mosquito.
questions.phonetic: /ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ɪz maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst. ðə ˈlɒŋɡɪst ˈrɪvər ɪz ðə naɪl. ðə moʊst ˈdeɪndʒərəs ˈænɪməl ɪz ðə məˈskiːtoʊ/
questions.hint: For short adjectives: 'the tallest', 'the longest'. For long adjectives: 'the most dangerous'. Always start with 'The' and use a full sentence with 'is'.
questions.explanation: World records are a fun and natural context for practising superlatives. This roleplay helps you produce complete superlative sentences with correct structure: 'The + superlative + noun + is + answer'.

questions.instruction: Say the following superlative adjective and its meaning in a full sentence. Focus on using the correct superlative form.
questions.audioPrompt: Let's practise superlative vocabulary. Please say this word in a full sentence. The word is 'the most expensive'. Use it to describe something you know.
questions.targetSentence: The most expensive phone in the shop is the newest iPhone.
questions.phonetic: /ðə moʊst ɪkˈspɛnsɪv foʊn ɪn ðə ʃɒp ɪz ðə ˈnjuːɪst ˈaɪfoʊn/
questions.hint: Remember: 'expensive' is a long adjective, so we say 'the most expensive', not 'the expensivest'. Stress 'MOST' and 'PEN' in 'ex-PEN-sive'.
questions.explanation: This drill checks that you know when to use 'the most + adjective' versus 'the + adjective-est'. Long adjectives (three or more syllables, and most two-syllable adjectives) use 'the most'. Short adjectives (one syllable, some two-syllable) use '-est'.

questions.instruction: Say the sentence with the correct superlative grammar. Change the adjective in brackets to the correct superlative form. The sentence is: 'This is (interesting) book I have ever read.'
questions.audioPrompt: Now let's check your grammar. I will give you a sentence with an adjective. You need to change it to the superlative form and say the complete sentence. Ready? 'This is [interesting] book I have ever read.' Say the full correct sentence now.
questions.targetSentence: This is the most interesting book I have ever read.
questions.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz ðə moʊst ˈɪntrəstɪŋ bʊk aɪ hæv ˈɛvər rɛd/
questions.hint: 'Interesting' has four syllables, so you must use 'the most interesting', not 'the interestingest'. Don't forget 'the' before 'most'.
questions.explanation: This grammar drill tests the rule: adjectives with three or more syllables always form the superlative with 'the most + adjective'. Common errors include forgetting 'the' or trying to add '-est' to long adjectives. The structure is: subject + is/are + the most + adjective + noun.

questions.instruction: Practise the syllable stress shift between the base adjective and its superlative form. Say both words clearly, stressing the correct syllable. First say 'exciting', then say 'the most exciting'.
questions.audioPrompt: Let's practise syllable stress. First, say the adjective 'exciting' — the stress is on the second syllable: ex-CI-ting. Now say the superlative form: 'the most exciting' — stress both 'MOST' and 'CI'. Say both forms now.
questions.targetSentence: Exciting. The most exciting.
questions.hint: In 'exciting', stress the middle syllable: ex-CI-ting. When you add 'the most', give a strong stress to 'MOST' as well. Do NOT stress 'the' — keep it weak: /ðə/.
questions.explanation: When forming superlatives with 'the most', the stress pattern shifts because you add a new stressed word ('most') before the adjective. The adjective keeps its original stress (ex-CI-ting), but now 'MOST' also receives stress. This creates a two-stress rhythm: 'the MOST ex-CI-ting'. Practise this rhythm to sound natural.

questions.instruction: Practise the difference between falling intonation (for statements) and rising intonation (for yes/no questions) when using superlative adjectives. Say both sentences clearly.
questions.audioPrompt: Now let's practise intonation. First, say this statement with falling intonation: 'Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world.' ↘ Your voice should go DOWN at the end. Now say this question with rising intonation: 'Is Mount Everest the tallest mountain in the world?' ↗ Your voice should go UP at the end. Say both sentences now.
questions.targetSentence: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. Is Mount Everest the tallest mountain in the world?
questions.phonetic: /maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst ɪz ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ↘/ — /ɪz maʊnt ˈɛvərɪst ðə ˈtɔːlɪst ˈmaʊntɪn ɪn ðə wɜːrld ↗/
questions.hint: For the statement, let your pitch fall on 'world' ↘. For the yes/no question, let your pitch rise on 'world?' ↗. The words are almost the same, but the intonation changes the meaning completely.
questions.explanation: Intonation is crucial for meaning in English. Statements use falling intonation (↘) to show you are giving information. Yes/no questions use rising intonation (↗) to show you are asking for confirmation. With superlative sentences, this distinction is especially important because the same words can be a fact or a question depending on your intonation.

practicumQuestions.question: In the passage, Rina says the book is 'the best gift.' What does 'the best' mean here?
options: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
It is a good gift, but not the number one gift.
It is a bad gift that she does not like.
practicumQuestions.answer: It is the number one gift — better than all other gifts she has received.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'The best' is the superlative form of 'good.' It means this gift is number one — it is better than ALL other gifts Rina has ever received. Superlatives always describe the top item in a group.

practicumQuestions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses a superlative for a LONG adjective?
options: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
The cheetah is the fastest animal on land.
The Amazon is the longest river in South America.
practicumQuestions.answer: The most expensive pizza in the world costs more than one thousand dollars.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Expensive' is a long adjective (three syllables), so it uses 'the most + adjective' to form the superlative: 'the most expensive.' The other two sentences use 'the -est' because 'fast' and 'long' are short adjectives.

practicumQuestions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.' What pattern does 'the highest' follow?
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'High' is a short adjective (one syllable), so its superlative form is 'the highest' — following the pattern 'the + adjective-est.' We do NOT say 'the most highest' because that is a double superlative and is incorrect.

practicumQuestions.question: According to the passage, why does Rina think her mom's fried rice is special?
options: Because she thinks it is the most delicious food, even though it is not the most expensive.
Because it is the most expensive food in the world.
Because her dad made it for her birthday.
practicumQuestions.answer: Because she thinks it is the most delicious food, even though it is not the most expensive.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Rina says: 'I think the most delicious food is my mom's fried rice. It is not the most expensive, but it is the best!' She loves it for the taste, not the price.

practicumQuestions.question: Choose the CORRECT superlative sentence based on what you learned in this reading mission.
options: The blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean.
The blue whale is most biggest animal in the ocean.
The blue whale is bigger animal in the ocean.
practicumQuestions.answer: The blue whale is the biggest animal in the ocean.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Big' is a short adjective, so the superlative is 'the biggest' (the + adjective-est). 'Most biggest' is wrong because you cannot use 'most' and '-est' together. 'Bigger' is a comparative form, not a superlative — it compares only two things.

practicumQuestions.question: In the passage, Rina mentions several superlative facts. How many different superlative adjectives can you find in the whole passage?
options: More than five different superlative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.answer: More than five different superlative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The passage contains many superlative adjectives: the best, the fastest, the highest, the most expensive, the most delicious, the longest, the biggest, and the most amazing. That is eight superlatives — definitely more than five!

practicumQuestions.question: Which word ALWAYS comes before a superlative adjective in English?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Superlative adjectives ALWAYS need 'the' before them. We say 'the tallest,' 'the best,' 'the most exciting' — never 'a tallest' or 'very tallest.' The word 'the' signals that we are talking about the number one item in a group.

practicumQuestions.question: Which question is grammatically correct?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Standard question order: Question Word + Auxiliary (do) + Subject (you) + Verb (live).

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 3 sentences about your school. Use a different superlative adjective in each sentence. Use one short adjective superlative, one long adjective superlative, and one irregular superlative.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must have 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must use a superlative adjective correctly. One sentence uses 'the + adjective-est', one uses 'the most + adjective', and one uses an irregular superlative (the best, the worst, or the farthest). All sentences must start with a capital letter and end with a period.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Mr. Andi is the tallest teacher in my school. The library is the most comfortable room in the building. My best friend is the best student in our class.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 4 sentences) about your family. Describe who is the tallest, the youngest, the best at cooking, or the most funny person. Use at least 3 superlative adjectives.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The answer must have at least 4 sentences about family members. At least 3 different superlative adjectives must be used correctly. Each superlative must include 'the'. Sentences must be capitalized and punctuated correctly. The paragraph must make sense and be about family.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: My father is the tallest person in my family. My little sister is the youngest. My mother is the best cook at home. My grandfather tells the most interesting stories of all.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 4 sentences comparing things in your city or town. Use superlative adjectives to describe the biggest building, the most popular food, the best place to visit, and the oldest building you know.

The student must use 'the' before each superlative. At least one short adjective superlative and one long adjective superlative must be included. Sentences must start with a capital letter and end with a period.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: The mall is the biggest building in my town. Nasi goreng is the most popular food here. The park is the best place to visit on weekends. The mosque near my house is the oldest building in my neighborhood.
